items.title: Presenting Your Figures: Data-informed Animated Transitions Across Scientific Figure Panels
items.abstract: Multi-panel figures are commonly used in research papers to show scientific data, and researchers often reuse them when presenting their work. Presenting these figures often involves explaining how data across chart panels are related. Animated transitions can progressively reveal these relationships, but two static panels specify only the endpoints, leaving what intermediate keyframes should show and how the transition should progress unclear. To support transition design across diverse scientific figures, we developed Figure Space and Transition Space through iterative analysis of 48 published multi-panel figures across eight scientific subject areas. Figure Space represents panel composition, data transformations, and visual encodings while retaining the links needed to trace panel results back to records. Transition Space uses this representation and source data to construct and sequence keyframes that make corresponding data visible and align them while preserving the meaning of each panel's position encodings. Building on these spaces, we developed FigFlux, a human-in-the-loop authoring system that guides AI agents in generating animated transitions from a multi-panel figure and its associated materials. Researchers can revise keyframes in natural language before animation generation. We evaluate FigFlux through cross-domain case studies, a study with 16 scientific authors, and expert assessment. Authors reported lower overall workload than with their familiar tools, while experts gave FigFlux transitions higher ratings than transitions created with participants' familiar tools or generated by AI alone. The example gallery have been published online: https://figflux.github.io.

items.title: Prevalence of Musculoskeletal Disorders among Shrimp Farm Workers
items.abstract: Aims: To assess the prevalence of musculoskeletal disorders among shrimp farm workers and examine their association with selected demographic characteristics. Study Design: A descriptive research design was adopted for the study. Place and Duration of Study: The study was conducted between 2023–2026 in the selected shrimp farming areas of Andhra Pradesh (Kakinada, West Godavari and Bapatla districts) and Telangana (Narayanpet, Jogulamba Gadwal and Wanaparthy districts). Methodology: A total of 150 shrimp farm workers were selected through purposive sampling based on their involvement in shrimp-farming activities. Data were collected using a researcher-developed structured interview schedule covering demographic and occupational characteristics and self-reported musculoskeletal disorders across different body regions. Frequencies, percentages, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and correlation analysis were used for statistical analysis. Results: Among the participants, 93.33 per cent were male and 68.67 per cent were engaged in elementary occupations. Upper back pain was frequently reported by 47.33 per cent of workers on the right side and 20 per cent on the left side. The corresponding percentages for lower back pain were 46 and 24 per cent, respectively, while wrist pain was reported by 44 per cent on the right side and 41.33 per cent on the left side. Muscle cramps were reported as occurring sometimes by 59.33 per cent on the right side and 55.33 per cent on the left side. Right-sided symptom scores were higher than left-sided scores, with a statistically significant difference between the two sides (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = −8.686, p < 0.001). A statistically significant difference was observed in overall musculoskeletal discomfort scores across the occupational groups (Kruskal–Wallis H = 7.163, df = 2, p = 0.028). Pearson’s correlation analysis showed no statistically significant relationships between overall MSD scores and age, education, socioeconomic status or monthly income (p > 0.05). Conclusion: The study highlighted the occurrence of musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) among shrimp farm workers and the need for attention to their occupational health. The findings provided a basis for identifying work-related ergonomic problems and developing suitable interventions, worker awareness programmes and regular health assessments to improve occupational health and safety in shrimp farming.

items.title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

items.title: ProactiMate: evaluating LLM-based chatbots for behavior change interventions
items.abstract: This paper explores the role of Large Language Models (LLMs) in promoting sustainable behavior, specifically in overcoming procrastination. Despite widespread recognition of the need for sustainable behavior change, individuals often struggle to break free from entrenched, unsustainable habits. LLMs, such as OpenAI’s GPT-4, represent a significant breakthrough in artificial intelligence and are increasingly used in behavior change interventions. This study introduces ProactiMate, a chatbot built using Motivational Interviewing (MI) principles and a Chain of Models approach for prompt engineering, designed to help users combat procrastination. Our research compares four LLMs (GPT-3.5 Turbo, LLaMA-3.2, Qwen-2.5, and SmolLM-1.7B) for output influence on procrastination avoidance, and assesses the impact of hyperparameters (temperature and top-p values) on procrastination avoidance. The findings reveal that GPT-3.5 outperforms other models across various evaluation metrics, and higher temperature and top-p values lead to more effective procrastination avoidance from automatic evaluation. According to expert evaluations, Qwen-2.5 and GPT-3.5 Turbo demonstrated notable effectiveness in fostering user engagement and motivation for addressing procrastination, with GPT-3.5 Turbo particularly distinguished by its capacity to provide strategies that help maintain long-term motivation. And GPT’s output aligns well with both automatic evaluation metrics and human evaluation. The results provide insights into the most effective ways to use LLMs in chatbot design, offering solutions for future usability testing.

items.abstract: Ushbu maqolada probatsiya nazoratidagi shaxslarning murojaatlari va iltimosnomalarini raqamlashtirishning dolzarb masalalari, amaliyotdagi mavjud muammolar hamda ularni bartaraf etish imkoniyatlari ilmiy-amaliy jihatdan tahlil qilinadi. Tadqiqotda inson omilini kamaytirish, takrorlanuvchi ish hajmini qisqartirish, shuningdek, protsessual va umumiy murojaatlar oʻrtasidagi huquqiy nomuvofiqliklarni hal etish masalalari yoritilgan. Maqolada sohaga oid konstitutsiyaviy normalar va "Jismoniy va yuridik shaxslarning murojaatlari toʻgʻrisida"gi Qonun amaliyoti tahlil qilinib, rivojlangan xorijiy davlatlar tajribasi qiyosiy oʻrganilgan hamda samarali raqamli integratsiya modelini joriy etish boʻyicha amaliy takliflar ilgari surilgan. В данной статье научно-практически анализируются актуальные вопросы цифровизации обращений и ходатайств лиц, находящихся под пробационным надзором, существующие проблемы в практике и пути их решения. В исследовании освещены возможности сокращения человеческого фактора, дублирования рабочей нагрузки, а также устранения правовых несоответствий между процессуальными и общими обращениями. В статье подробно анализируются конституционные нормы и практическое применение Закона «Об обращениях физических и юридических лиц», проводится comparative-оценка зарубежного опыта и разрабатываются практические предложения по внедрению эффективной модели цифровой интеграции. This article provides a scientific and practical analysis of the digitization of applications and petitions of individuals under probation supervision, identifying current operational challenges and potential solutions. The research highlights strategies to minimize the human factor, reduce duplicated administrative workloads, and resolve legal discrepancies between procedural and general inquiries. Furthermore, the study examines relevant constitutional provisions and the practical application of the Law "On Appeals of Physical and Legal Entities," comparatively evaluates international practices, and presents concrete proposals for implementing an integrated digital framework.

items.title: PROPIEDADES PSICOMÉTRICAS DE LA ESCALA DE COMPROMISO HACIA LAS TAREAS ESCOLARES EN ESTUDIANTES DE NIVEL PRIMARIA DE UGEL SANTA, 2026
items.abstract: This study aimed to determine the psychometric properties of the School Task Engagement Scale (ECTE) among primary school students from UGEL Santa, 2026. A basic, quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional study with a descriptive-instrumental scope was conducted. The sample consisted of 300 fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-grade students selected through proportional stratified probability sampling. Data were collected through a survey using the 18-item ECTE, which measures affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement. Content validity was assessed by five experts, yielding an overall Aiken’s V of 1.00 for clarity, relevance, and coherence. The three-factor model showed acceptable fit indices (χ²/df = 2.18; RMSEA = 0.063; SRMR = 0.044; CFI = 0.921; TLI = 0.909), and factor loadings were above 0.50. Cronbach’s alpha values for the dimensions ranged from 0.765 to 0.787, while McDonald’s omega ranged from 0.766 to 0.792. The overall scale yielded α = 0.914 and ω = 0.916. The findings provide favorable evidence of validity and reliability in the studied sample, although generalization to other populations requires further research.

items.abstract: Protokół zadania 0.4 programu badawczego monografii „Świadomość sytuacyjna na rynku mieszkaniowym. Rama pojęciowa, narzędzie pomiaru i program badawczy“, wraz z aneksami nr 1 i nr 2, wynikiem rozpoznania zbiorów oraz audytem katalogów zmiennych programu HFCS. Zadanie przewidywało częściowy i zastępczy test dwóch hipotez rdzeniowych — H-C o miskalibracji kompetencji oraz H-E o spójności międzypoziomowej — na danych panelowych pochodzących ze zbiorów istniejących. Protokół określa zmienne wymagane, zbiory do sprawdzenia i regułę rozstrzygania przed przystąpieniem do rozpoznania. Rozpoznanie zamknięto wynikiem negatywnym w zakresie krajowym. Żaden ze sprawdzonych zbiorów obejmujących Polskę nie zawiera pomiaru horyzontu planowania gospodarstwa domowego, będącego pierwszym składnikiem wskaźnika różnicowego wymaganego przez H-E, ani obiektywnego pomiaru kompetencji finansowej, co wyklucza również H-C. The review closed with a null result for Poland: none of the datasets examined measures the household planning horizon, nor does any contain an objective measure of financial competence. The audit shows that the two components of the differential indicator required by hypothesis H-E were never simultaneously available in any of the five HFCS waves. items.title: Psychological reward and physiological demand in virtual cycling: an exploratory within-subject study
items.abstract: Virtual environments are often added to exercise equipment to make exercise more engaging, although previous work has often emphasised enjoyment. This exploratory within-subject study compared stationary cycling with screen-based virtual cycling in 15 adults (6 women, 9 men; aged 20–59 years). Each participant completed one 10-min, self-paced session in each condition, in counterbalanced order, on the same recumbent bicycle with fixed resistance. After each session, participants completed the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory and rated their perceived exertion (Borg 6–20); heart rate and cadence were recorded every minute. Enjoyment was higher after virtual cycling (mean difference 2.31 points on a 1–7 scale, 95% CI [1.61, 3.00]), as was value/usefulness (1.38 [0.56, 2.20]); 14 and 12 participants, respectively, reported higher scores. Both paired t-test differences remained after Holm correction. Differences in perceived competence, effort/importance, and pressure/tension were smaller, with confidence intervals including zero. Heart rate (4.9 bpm, 95% CI [-0.04, 9.8]) and cadence (2.8 rpm [-2.4, 7.9]) showed no clear difference between conditions. Perceived exertion was slightly higher during virtual cycling (0.8 points [0.01, 1.59]), but this difference did not remain after correction. Power output was not measured, so workload could not be compared directly. Enjoyment was strongly correlated with value/usefulness during virtual cycling (r = 0.87, 95% CI [0.64, 0.95]); individual responses also varied, particularly in perceived competence. Given the small sample and single 10-min session per condition, larger studies should measure workload directly and examine responses across repeated sessions.

items.title: Query-Aware vs. Query-Agnostic Training-Free Video Token Pruning in Multimodal LLMs
items.abstract: Video Large Language Models process large numbers of visual tokens, making token pruning important for efficient inference. Training-free pruning methods differ in whether and how they use the user query, and the value of query conditioning remains unclear. We present a controlled study of training-free, pre-LLM video token selection. Using a shared Qwen-3-VL backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings, we compare 21 pruning principles spanning query-agnostic, shallow query-conditioned, structured query-conditioned, and holistic strategies. To instantiate the last two categories, we introduce Structured Query Pruning, which decomposes the question into semantic anchors, and a Pareto variant, which combines anchor relevance with query-agnostic visual diversity. Across Video-MME, MVBench, and LongVideoBench, relevance computed from the raw question embedding is unreliable (8--16 points below the best methods), whereas anchors derived from query decomposition avoid this failure. However, query access is not inherently advantageous: strong query-agnostic coverage methods remain competitive or superior in the full-field comparison. Relative to a redundancy-only baseline, structured selection helps most on evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; on broad tasks, the holistic selector improves over either relevance or redundancy alone. Further, pruning reduces cost and memory. These results support a practical design rule: preserve visual coverage by default, and add structured relevance when the task and token budget demand selective evidence retrieval.

items.title: R-SYS for protocol versioning and independent reviewer workflows in systematic reviews
items.abstract: Background Systematic review software must coordinate independent human decisions, protocol amendments and heterogeneous information sources. Synchronizing reviewers at every stage can create waiting time unrelated to the scientific assessment of a record. We describe R-SYS, a workflow that links decisions to versioned protocols and allows reviewers to progress independently before a final reconciliation step. Methods The reference implementation combines an eleven-phase guarded lifecycle, immutable locked protocol versions, deterministic rendering of a canonical search strategy, per-reviewer working sets and decision provenance. Each primary reviewer advances through title and abstract screening, full-text assessment, extraction and risk-of-bias appraisal using their own preceding decisions, subject to human adjudication. A final convergence checkpoint resolves outstanding work before synthesis. Artificial intelligence (AI) supplies advisory recommendations that are excluded from human reconciliation. We analyse completion times under explicit scheduling assumptions and describe implementation limitations. Results With identical task sets, continuous reviewer availability and no external waiting, independent lanes achieve a completion time equal to the largest reviewer workload. This is a lower bound for schedules that impose additional synchronization constraints. Disagreement can introduce superseded work and delays; a sufficient condition for retaining an advantage over stage barriers is stated. The implementation provides mechanisms for protocol change control, reviewer coordination and traceable reporting. No empirical measurements of accuracy, efficiency, usability or cost are reported. Conclusions R-SYS provides a reference design for separating reviewer independence from workflow synchronization. Its theoretical scheduling properties do not establish practical time savings, search completeness or AI accuracy. A separate, prospectively specified validation study is planned after completed reviews using the platform become available.

items.title: Radiologist Workstation Configuration Preferences: Converging Evidence Toward Best Practices
items.abstract: Diagnostic radiologists spend much of their professional time interpreting imaging studies using a variety of workstation and monitor configurations. Despite well-established ergonomic principles, there are no widely accepted recommendations regarding monitor configuration, application placement, or peripheral device selection. This variability, particularly across academic medical centers with diverse workstation configurations, may contribute to musculoskeletal injury, workflow inefficiency, cognitive burden, and challenges integrating artificial intelligence (AI) applications. This study characterizes radiologist workstation configurations and determines whether similar usage patterns emerge across two independent national needs assessments. The findings from both assessments were compared. The first consisted of live audience polling during an RSNA 2025 educational session on radiologist ergonomics (n = 54). The second was an online survey distributed through professional LinkedIn and radiology social media communities (n = 49). Survey questions evaluated monitor number and orientation, workstation layout, application placement, ergonomic practices, sit-stand workstation use, and peripheral devices. Both assessments demonstrated similar workstation preferences. Most respondents in both the RSNA poll (n = 54) and online needs assessment (n = 49) used four-monitor equivalent configurations consisting of two portrait diagnostic monitors (often combined into one 30″ landscape) flanked by two supplemental monitors. Dictation was most commonly displayed on the left supplemental monitor, adjacent to the current examination (on the left diagnostic monitor). Respondents reported diverse placement of worklists, thumbnails, AI tools, peer review, electronic medical records, and advanced visualization applications. Sit-stand workstations were widely used, with most respondents standing 10-30% of the workday. Gaming mice with hyperscrolling functionality were the predominant pointing devices with very similar functions (window/level, measure, arrow, zoom/pan, and ROI). Two independent national needs assessments revealed consistent patterns in radiologist workstation configurations despite differences in survey methodology and participant populations. These findings suggest an emerging, flexible de facto standard that could guide ergonomic recommendations, workstation design and procurement, residency training, workflow optimization, and AI integration.

items.title: Real-Time Academic Platform Integration Design (RAPID): A Descriptive Framework for Course Communication and Support
items.abstract: Persistent, channel-organized communication environments give instructors ways to arrange questions, assistance, announcements, and informal interaction alongside a learning management system. Their use depends on how students enter the environment, how information and audiences are organized, who provides assistance, and how participation is experienced. This conceptual article presents Real-Time Academic Platform Integration Design (RAPID), a descriptive framework developed through a focused synthesis of 37 publications and a source-anchored matrix of 750 evidence items. Following a bounded literature search with artificial intelligence support for screening and extraction, the authors reviewed source evidence and selected and refined the framework by comparing model-generated alternatives. RAPID comprises four components: Student Onboarding, Environment Organization, Sustainable Help, and Student Participation and Social Climate, interpreted through an affordance perspective and Community of Inquiry. A constructed LMS-centered baseline, two reflective teaching illustrations, and a literature-informed projection show how it applies across differences in course size, staffing, and participation requirements. The framework’s usefulness, workload implications, and relationship to learning require empirical study.

items.title: Reclaiming Agency in Introductory Business Education: A Process-Oriented Framework for AI Governance, Risk, and Inclusive Pedagogy
items.abstract: Introduction to Business is often a student’s first encounter with how organizations plan, take risks, communicate, and answer for their decisions. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how students research and write, and how colleges increasingly recognize neurodiverse ways of learning. Together these make the first business course a natural place to reconsider what introductory business education can be. This paper describes a redesign of BUS 101 at Barton College’s School of Business & Innovation, being delivered in Fall 2026 across three sections taught by three instructors. The redesign treats the course itself as a working business environment. Syllabus policies become exercises in applied risk ethics: a “24-Hour High-Risk Window” and a one-time “Stuff Happens Pass” modeled on a contingency reserve. Academic integrity rests on process rather than detection, through visible revision histories and a Socratic oral defense. Presentations carry 40% of the grade, personal finance is taught as a form of self-governance and a gateway to business finance, and qualitative video reflections complement numerical ratings. Shared cross-section sessions with industry speakers provide continuity while preserving each instructor’s approach. Drawing on process philosophy, the ethics of responsibility, and experiential learning theory, we set out the design’s rationale, its implementation to date, and a research agenda whose results will be reported in a follow-up study.

items.title: Recommendations for Incorporating Large Language Models Into Psychological Research: A Commentary on Austin et al. (2025)
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have clear potential to contribute to psychological research methods. However, as with any new research method, LLM-based methods require rigorous evaluation. Towards this end, Austin and colleagues evaluated the ability of two LLMs (GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash) to facilitate scale validation by identifying relevant criterion measures and generating validity hypotheses for assessing convergent and discriminant validity. We argue that their study has several key limitations that limit the conclusions that can be drawn about the proposed method's suitability for use in validation research. We situate our critique within three recommendations for incorporating LLMs into research: (a) avoid essentialisation and overgeneralisation about 'AI', (b) use application programming interfaces when evaluating LLMs in research contexts and (c) evaluate LLM-based methods using clearly specified criteria. Finally, we consider whether adopting the proposed method might reinforce or amplify existing limitations in the psychological literature, namely, the proliferation of overlapping constructs and inadequately validated measures.

items.title: Recoverability-Centered Trajectory Governance for Long-Horizon Clinical AI Agents
items.abstract: Clinical AI is moving from systems that generate discrete predictions and recommendations toward agents capable of pursuing clinical objectives through repeated tool use, communication, planning, and state-changing actions. Emerging systems support multistep electronic health record workflows, and increasingly envision longitudinal care across repeated encounters. This transition expands safety assessment beyond discrete outputs and actions. Through its actions, an agent can help create the clinical state on which its subsequent decisions depend. Consequently, individually defensible actions may compose into an unsafe trajectory, even when no single action is clearly erroneous. We propose recoverability-centered trajectory governance as a clinical synthesis of established safety approaches, linking patient-specific corrective capacity to the continuing justification for delegated authority. Its central objective is clinical recoverability: preserving the opportunity for the human-AI care system to redirect care before clinically acceptable corrective pathways are exhausted. We define recovery margin as the remaining opportunity for such correction, and reauthorization boundaries as conditions requiring delegated authority to end or narrow pending renewed human judgment. This framing distinguishes reversibility, primarily a property of an action, from recoverability, a property of an evolving clinical trajectory. The operational framework combines persistent obligation tracking, independent monitoring, explicit reauthorization, authority contraction, graceful degradation, independent escalation, and verified human takeover. Oversight should concentrate at consequential trajectory junctions. Evaluation should combine trajectory stress testing, component-specific recovery-margin indicators, interruption-and-takeover testing, and population-level surveillance. Trajectory governance complements product lifecycle oversight by examining whether continued patient-specific delegation remains justified as care evolves. Because corrective capacity depends partly on access to timely monitoring and human rescue, recoverability is also an equity issue. The defining safety question is therefore not only whether an action is acceptable but whether continued delegation remains justified. The proposed indicators and governance mechanisms require domain-specific operationalization and empirical validation, including comparison with established safeguards.

items.title: Reducing barriers to inclusive tertiary STEM education: opportunities for AI
items.abstract: Australia’s growing demand for science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) skills contrasts with stagnant tertiary participation and persistent inequities. This brief review examines barriers to inclusive tertiary STEM education and the potential for artificial intelligence (AI) to support Universal Design for Learning. AI can provide multimodal content, personalised scaffolding, flexible participation and assessment, and support for self-regulated and collaborative learning. items.title: Regional artificial intelligence development and agricultural ecological efficiency: evidence from Chinese provinces
items.abstract: Existing studies have primarily focused on the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on productivity and carbon emission efficiency, while systematic evidence on whether and through which mechanisms AI improves agricultural ecological efficiency (AEE) remains relatively limited. Using provincial panel data from China for the period 2005 to 2023, this study employs the entropy weighting method to measure regional AI development and a slack-based measure (SBM) model incorporating undesirable outputs to evaluate AEE. A two-way fixed effects model is further constructed to examine the effects of AI on AEE and the underlying mechanisms. AI is conceptually distinct from general digitalization, automation, precision agriculture, and information technology development, as its defining feature lies in leveraging machine learning, intelligent sensing, and algorithmic decision-making to achieve more advanced data processing and intelligent decision-making capabilities. The results indicate that a 0.1-unit increase in regional AI development is associated with an average increase of 0.01078 units in AEE. Mechanism analysis suggests that AI can indirectly improve AEE by promoting green finance development and industrial structure upgrading. Furthermore, agricultural technological innovation exhibits a significant threshold effect, with higher levels of technological innovation strengthening the positive effect of AI on AEE. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the positive effect of AI on AEE is more pronounced in eastern regions, regions with lower levels of urbanization and agricultural modernization, and non-major grain-producing regions. Further analysis identifies positive spatial spillover effects of AI on AEE in neighboring regions, contributing to coordinated green agricultural development across local and neighboring regions. This study provides evidence on the effects, transmission mechanisms, and threshold conditions through which AI improves AEE, offering new empirical insights into the role of AI in facilitating the green transformation of agriculture and extending the analytical perspective of agricultural sustainability research.

items.title: Reinforcement-Aligned Probabilistic Weather Forecasting with Discrete Tokens
items.abstract: Global medium-range weather forecasting must not only generate ensembles efficiently to characterize uncertainty in future states, but also serve downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations. We introduce WeatherCraft, a framework that unifies probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment through discrete weather tokens, bringing the GPT-style pretraining--post-training paradigm to global medium-range weather forecasting. A multiscale tokenizer represents atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine token hierarchy, while a Transformer models causal dependencies across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Direct sampling generates diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities enable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On the ERA5 benchmark, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, achieves an approximately $18\times$ inference speedup over GenCast. Direct fair-CRPS adaptation improves ensemble probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes. This work establishes discrete autoregressive modeling as a general foundation for scalable, task-alignable Earth system foundation models.

items.title: ReLay: Bidirectional Layout-Code Translation and Library Evolution for Reusable and Process-Portable Analog Design
items.abstract: Analog layout generators provide a programmable interface for design reuse and process migration, but their coverage is limited by handcrafted libraries. The designer knowledge embedded in complete layouts remains implicit in their geometry, making it difficult to capture in reusable generator libraries. We present ReLay, a bidirectional layout-code framework that recovers generator programs from existing layouts, enabling cross-PDK portability and parametric resizing of existing designs. Constructions that recur across recovered programs are promoted to library functions, so the library evolves as layouts accumulate. We also introduce the first layout-code benchmark: 1,050 hand-drawn layouts from 27 circuit families across three open-source PDKs, ranging from primitive cells to full chips. Learned functions account for 53-66% of layout-building calls in held-out layouts, demonstrating reuse beyond the learning corpus. Frontier LLM agents use ReLay to produce new layouts at 64-77% lower API cost per completed task than direct geometry generation, with comparable completion rates and electrical quality.

items.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
items.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

items.title: Reproducible Python Code and Experimental Results for AI-Based Bearing Fault Classification Using Vibration Sensor Data: Effects of Signal Representations and Decision Thresholds
items.abstract: This repository provides the complete Python implementation and verified experimental results associated with the research article entitled “AI-Based Bearing Fault Classification Using Vibration Sensor Data: Effects of Signal Representations and Decision Thresholds.” The study investigates the effects of dimensionless vibration features, signal representations, physical-time dynamics, and source-derived decision thresholds on artificial intelligence-based bearing fault classification. Experiments were conducted using 59 source recordings from the MCC5–THU three-phase asynchronous motor dataset and 32 target recordings from the University of Ottawa Electric Motor Dataset. Five predefined feature and temporal configurations, 11 classification models, and four decision rules were evaluated. The models include physical-time spiking neural networks, a memoryless SNN counterpart, conventional machine learning classifiers, and ensemble methods. Model training, calibration, and decision threshold selection were performed exclusively on source data using nested stratified group cross-validation with three outer folds and two inner folds. The trained models were evaluated on the Ottawa recordings without target-side parameter updates. The Ottawa analyses include exploratory comparisons at the recording level. The archive contains: The complete Python source code and software dependencies. Publication Figures 5–10 in PNG and SVG formats. Publication Tables 5–8 in CSV format. Source cross-validation results and record-level predictions. Ottawa classification scores, calibration results, and decision thresholds. Group-based bootstrap results and supporting feature statistics. Experimental protocol, raw-data checksums, software environment information, and reproducibility verification reports. Numerical results were checked against the manuscript at the reported precision. The archive also includes independent verification of metrics recalculated from serialized prediction files. The original raw vibration recordings are not redistributed. They remain accessible through the original dataset repositories. Original datasets: MCC5–THU: https://doi.org/10.17632/6s3dggj9mw.1 University of Ottawa Electric Motor Dataset: https://doi.org/10.17632/msxs4vj48g.2 This repository supports transparent evaluation, independent verification, and reproducibility of the reported experimental findings.

items.title: Rethinking EFL teachers’ readiness for AI integration in online language teaching
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into online language teaching has gained increasing attention due to its potential to enhance instructional efficiency, provide real-time feedback, and support personalized learning in EFL contexts. However, previous research has typically focused on teachers’ perceptions, readiness or challenges in using AI separately from one another, resulting in a fragmented picture of AI adoption. The present study investigates EFL teachers’ understanding of AI, the context-specific variables affecting their readiness for deploying it, and the barriers to incorporating it in online language teaching. Using semi-structured interviews with nine EFL teachers, a qualitative case study design was used, and analysis of the data was by means of thematic methods. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study aims to understand teachers’ adoption and integration of AI Tools. The results show that teachers tend to perceive AI as a learning assistant and efficiency-oriented tool, which represents autonomous and flexible modes of learning. However, several barriers persist, including limited conceptual understanding of AI, difficulties in selecting appropriate tools, pedagogical and ethical concerns regarding student over-reliance and academic integrity, and technical constraints. The study highlights important pedagogical implications, suggesting the need for targeted professional development, clearer instructional guidelines, and institutional support to promote effective and responsible AI integration in EFL classrooms.

items.title: Rethinking English Education In The Era Of Generative Ai And Global Englishes
items.abstract: The advent of generative AI has provoked an ontological crisis in language education, tempting policymakers to equate machine-generated output with human interpretive capacity. This article challenges the premise that such technologies render language learning obsolete, arguing instead that an AI-saturated landscape makes robust humanistic engagement more vital than ever. Addressing the “scholar’s dilemma,” the paper proposes a structural shift in higher education from traditional silos toward horizontal, cross-disciplinary integration. Because English functions as a global lingua franca (ELF) and exerts an algorithmic hegemony over large language models (LLMs), advanced proficiency remains indispensable for critically querying these platforms. We advocate for a pedagogical evolution from the mechanical transmission of referential information (informing) to facilitating imaginative exploration (engaging). Central to this shift is the reclamation of “literature with a small l” as the primary representational material used to cultivate students’ “textual power.” By prioritizing the interpretive struggle over cognitive offloading—a tension described here as the “Picasso Paradox”—educators can formalize a “fifth skill” (complex critical thinking in English). This framework provides the cognitive foundation for students to navigate an AI-saturated world not as passive users, but as active curators equipped with ethical discernment and epistemic agency.

items.title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining
items.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7% and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.

items.title: Rubric Semantics or Numerical Priors? Auditing Scale-Direction Bias in LLM Judges
items.abstract: Recent benchmark evaluations increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) as automatic judges. This paradigm assumes LLMs evaluate based on the rubric's semantic meaning rather than its numeric scale. We question this assumption by introducing semantic faithfulness: the principle that semantically equivalent rubrics must yield consistent scores. To quantify this, we propose a scale-reversal probe that inverts score anchors without altering evaluation criteria. Furthermore, we introduce floor normalization to calibrate reversal disagreement against intrinsic model variability, enabling fair cross-model comparisons. Experiments across five meta-evaluation benchmarks with seven diverse LLM judges spanning open-weight and proprietary models reveal widespread violations of semantic faithfulness, showing that raw reversal agreement alone is misleading. Finally, we demonstrate that bidirectional anchor averaging reduces dependence on any single anchor direction without compromising alignment with human judgments. Our findings emphasize that trustworthy LLM judges must reliably follow rubric semantics, not just correlate with human ratings.

items.title: RULE-LLM reporting framework for large language model-as-a-judge evaluation in medicine developed from a scoping review
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate other models’ outputs in medicine, an approach known as LLM-as-a-Judge (LaaJ), yet no LaaJ-specific reporting checklist exists. This scoping review included 91 medical LaaJ studies: 69 from 5,571 database records and 22 from a previous review. Judges were mainly used for response evaluation (74.7%), and 76.9% of the studies used at least one proprietary LLM. Agreement with human evaluators was reported in 65.9% of the studies, with widely varying metrics. Based on these findings, this study developed RULE-LLM, a reporting framework of 21 items and eight sub-items across four domains: role and task specification, underlying data and criteria, LLM-Judge design and output, and evaluation of judge performance. items.title: Safety and health of app-based food delivery riders: A scoping review
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of app-based food delivery has intensified concerns about riders’ road safety and occupational health. This scoping review maps and synthesises existing research on the safety of food delivery riders, including its methodological characteristics, multilevel determinants, safety and health outcomes, and prevention approaches. Following the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, and TRID were searched for English-language sources published from 2013 to 2026. After duplicate removal and two stage screening, 198 sources were included and synthesised through descriptive mapping and thematic analysis. The evidence comprised surveys, interviews, observations, naturalistic riding studies, platform data, and retrospective hospital and crash records. The evidence base was dominated by cross-sectional and self-reported research. Research activity in this field surged from 2022. Findings indicate that rider safety and health are shaped by interacting determinants at four levels: individual characteristics; work and platform conditions; road, vehicle, and environmental conditions; and institutional and social protection. Reported outcomes extended beyond risky riding, crashes, and traffic injuries to include musculoskeletal symptoms, fatigue, sleep disturbance, environmental exposure, and psychological distress. Only a small proportion of studies evaluated implemented interventions, leaving the effectiveness of platform, infrastructure, and policy level measures uncertain. Current evidence remains geographically concentrated, methodologically heterogeneous, and limited in its capacity to establish causal relationships. Improving rider safety therefore requires a shared, systems-based approach involving riders, platforms, restaurants, customers, transport authorities, and labour regulators, alongside longitudinal, exposure-adjusted, and intervention focused research.

items.title: Same Judgement, Different Scores: Numerical Scoring Topology in LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
items.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used as automated evaluators to reduce the cost and time required for human annotation. However, the role of scoring-scheme design in the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation remains underexplored. To address this problem, we introduce numerical scoring topology, which characterizes the structural design of a scoring scheme in terms of its scale width, granularity, offset, symmetry, and boundary placement. Building on this definition, we conduct the first systematic study of how numerical scoring topology influences zero-shot LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation across diverse benchmarks and judge models. Our results show that numerical scoring topology systematically affects judge scores, calibration, and robustness, particularly in judgment-intensive evaluations. Shifted and narrow ranges tend to induce some of the largest score deviations across many settings. We further find that stronger and larger judge models generally achieve higher discriminative validity and greater robustness to scoring-topology changes. These findings suggest that numerical scoring topology should be treated as an integral component of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation and highlight the need for more principled and standardized scoring protocols.

items.title: SCARVA: Interpretable Agentic Reasoning in Software Supply-Chain Analysis
items.abstract: Complex applications may inherit security vulnerabilities from their dependencies, though a vulnerable dependency does not necessarily endanger the application. Existing tools flag dependencies associated with public vulnerabilities, and more advanced ones analyze the call graph to assess whether the vulnerable code is reachable. However, these approaches are limited to specific programming languages and ecosystems. LLM agents are promising candidates for this task, yet they hallucinate, take shortcuts, and reward hack. As these behaviors are opaque, the agents' conclusions may not be trusted. We present SCARVA a framework designed to produce interpretable reports. SCARVA combines advanced agent reasoning with an evidence-collection methodology that assesses the agent's analysis and improves its trustworthiness. Specifically, the ANALYST performs a software security assessment while SCARVA records every tool call, file access, and web request. Then, one or more independent JUDGE agents inspect the ANALYST's result and produce an evidence-backed report. We evaluate SCARVA on 54 manually curated cases, balanced across exploitable, non-exploitable, and vulnerability-free projects, using both open-weight and frontier models. The best ANALYST model, Qwen 3.8, reaches 82% balanced accuracy and surpasses the evaluated proprietary models. Human annotation validates the JUDGE findings: Claude Opus 5.5 performs best, agreeing with annotators in 94% of claim checks. Finally, we discuss the most common failure modes of agents on supply-chain vulnerability assessment.

items.abstract: Science communication leverages online multimedia to raise public awareness of research and discovery, yet its efficacy is built upon digital competencies, communication and storytelling. These skills sit outside the scope of traditional scientific training, and artificial intelligence (AI) tools can accelerate professional learning in service of public outreach. Three different AI prompting strategies were used to convert a research article written by the author to a format appropriate for a public lecture. Different titles, graphics, and a talk outline informed by the Three Act Storytelling framework were extracted from the paper using one-shot, chain of thought and role-prompting strategies. These resources can be re-purposed for video abstracts, lay summaries and social media posts to facilitate science communication to a broad generalist audience. The effectiveness of AI as a collaborative tool for ideation is considered alongside its impact on scientific credibility and graduate employability.

items.title: Scite.ai and Education 5.0: Advancing AI Readiness, Research Literacy, and Evidence-Based Academic Practice Through Smart Citations
items.abstract: Education 5.0 places human agency, ethical technology use, critical thinking, creativity, and meaningful learning at the centre of digital transformation. In higher education, this shift requires institutions to develop not only technological infrastructure but also the research and information literacies needed to evaluate AI-mediated knowledge. Scite.ai is an AI-enabled scholarly citation-intelligence platform that extends conventional citation indexing by displaying citation context and classifying citation statements as supporting, contrasting, or mentioning. This chapter critically examines how Scite can contribute to AI readiness, research literacy, evidence evaluation, and responsible academic practice within an Education 5.0 ecosystem. An integrative review approach is used to synthesize Scite-specific research with literature on Education 5.0, AI literacy, information literacy, technology acceptance, human-centred AI, academic integrity, and institutional governance. The chapter argues that Scite should not be positioned as an automated authority or replacement for scholarly reading. Rather, it can function as an evidence-navigation and critical-reading layer within a broader institutional learning ecosystem. A new institutional conceptual framework is proposed in which Education 5.0 provides the normative context; institutional and stakeholder readiness provide enabling conditions; technology acceptance influences use; Scite-supported practices provide research affordances; and AI literacy, information literacy, critical evaluation, and evidence synthesis mediate potential outcomes. The framework is operationalized through a six-stage institutional roadmap: diagnose, prepare, pilot, integrate, evaluate, and scale. The chapter also identifies risks related to classification error, incomplete coverage, contextual ambiguity, automation bias, privacy, affordability, and academic integrity. The central conclusion is that the educational value of Scite depends less on automation itself than on the quality of human-AI interaction, pedagogical design, verification practices, and institutional governance surrounding its use.

items.title: SegAnyFruit: Learning Generalizable and Edge Deployable Fruit Instance Segmentation at Scale
items.abstract: Deploying fruit instance segmentation in real agricultural settings requires generalizing across unseen species, orchards, and imaging conditions under strict onboard compute and annotation budgets. We introduce SegAnyFruit (SAF), a data construction and progressive training framework that distills foundation-model priors into lightweight, prompt-free segmenters. SAF combines generic mask pre-training, broad mid-training on automatically annotated web imagery from our curated WebFruits dataset, and human-verified agricultural refinement post-training on PaperFruits, together spanning 733K images and 9.66M whole-fruit masks across 165 fruit types. Across seven benchmarks, zero-shot SAF-RF-DETR-XL reaches 69.06 average mask AP50:95 (+4.76 over SAM 3) while remaining deployable on edge devices. SAF initialization also boosts few-shot to full-shot adaptation across five agricultural domains while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we systematically analyze training stages, data scale, model capacity, and generative augmentation, and validate our pipeline's transferability to underwater, cell, and human segmentation. We will release our datasets, code, and SAF models.

items.title: Segurança dos profissionais que atuam no serviço de atendimento pré-hospitalar (SAMU): revisão integrativa
items.abstract: Introduction: Mobile pre-hospital care plays a fundamental role in emergency and urgent healthcare assistance, being responsible for rapid and decisive interventions in life-threatening situations. In this context, health professionals working in Mobile Intensive Care Units are constantly exposed to different occupational risks, including biological, physical, ergonomic and psychosocial hazards resulting from the dynamic and unpredictable conditions of the work environment. Objective: To analyze the factors related to the safety of health professionals working in mobile pre-hospital care, with emphasis on occupational risks present in Mobile Intensive Care Units. Methodology: This is an integrative literature review, with a descriptive character and qualitative approach, carried out in the databases Virtual Health Library, LILACS, BDENF, SciELO and PubMed/MEDLINE. Full scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025, in Portuguese, English and Spanish, related to the proposed theme, were included. Results and Discussions: The analyzed studies showed that professionals working in mobile pre-hospital care are frequently exposed to accidents involving biological material, urban violence, traffic accidents, physical exhaustion, emotional overload and high levels of occupational stress. Furthermore, inadequate working conditions, insufficient material resources and limitations related to continuous training contribute to increasing the occupational vulnerability of these teams. On the other hand, the studies highlighted the importance of biosafety measures, proper use of Personal Protective Equipment, continuing education and strengthening institutional policies aimed at workers' health. Final considerations: It is concluded that occupational risks present in mobile pre-hospital care directly impact the health and quality of life of professionals, highlighting the need to strengthen protection strategies and occupational health promotion in urgent and emergency healthcare services.

items.title: Self-Reflection and Self-Correction in Agentic AI: A Critical Review of Feedback, Verification, Memory, and Failure Modes
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence transforms self-correction from a localized answer-revision problem into a system-level reliability and recovery challenge. In autonomous, stateful, and long-horizon systems, early errors can propagate through reasoning, planning, retrieval, tool use, external actions, multi-agent interaction, and persistent memory. However, existing research often treats self-correction as either response-level refinement or a capability within broader agent architectures. This study develops an agent-level perspective that connects these fragmented views. It distinguishes reasoning, reflection, verification, correction, and adaptation, emphasizing that reasoning or critique alone does not constitute self-correction unless evaluative information produces a subsequent behavioral change. The study introduces a unified corrective lifecycle covering anomaly detection, error diagnosis and localization, corrective evidence acquisition, repair, validation, commitment or rollback, memory updating, and continuation, termination, or escalation. Existing approaches are organized across five dimensions: correction target, feedback source, temporal scope, persistence, and control architecture. A comparative synthesis shows that self-correction is not uniformly beneficial: repeated reflection can improve performance, stagnate, or degrade initially correct behavior. More reliable gains generally arise when feedback is task-relevant, informative, and at least partially independent of the process that produced the error. The study also identifies key failure modes, including missed errors, unsuccessful repair, over-correction, error amplification, memory contamination, and objective misalignment. These findings motivate research on calibrated intervention, memory integrity, verification, rollback, cost-aware correction, human escalation, and resilience under distribution shift.

items.title: Semantic Basketball Querying and Temporal Grounding of Play-by-Play Events in Broadcast Video
items.abstract: Basketball play-by-play data provide semi-structured descriptions of game events, but connecting analytical queries to the corresponding moments in broadcast video remains challenging. Towards this direction, this paper presents a semantic framework that integrates basketball play-by-play information into a Knowledge Graph (KG) through the BBall ontology, and links recorded events to temporally grounded video segments using scoreboard-based optical character recognition (OCR). The framework supports multimodal exploitation using structured queries over game events, through the research prototype CourtLens. The latter enables users to retrieve relevant video evidence through a unified semantic interface, including interactive shot charts, filters, SPARQL queries, and natural-language questions through LLM-to-SPARQL. The underlying KG contains 9.5 M play-by-play-related triples covering 1063 games, while the interactive video catalogue currently provides synchronized access to 28 games from 3 EuroLeague seasons. Concerning evaluation, a manually annotated benchmark of 1833 actions from three EuroLeague games yields an overall median absolute temporal error of 4.0 s, with 57.72% and 68.46% of all actions localized within 5 s and 10 s, respectively. Notably, running-clock events (missed/made field goals, assists, rebounds, blocks, steals and turnovers) achieve higher accuracy with 81.04% localized within 5 s and 90.47% within 10 s, demonstrating the system’s effectiveness in temporally grounding actions during active gameplay. Finally, the offline grounding pipeline processes video at 22.74× real time, whereas the interactive CourtLens web application offers real-time interaction for video analysis, e.g., less than 1 s for filter-based search.

items.title: Sequential Gaussian Codebooks for Covariance-Aware Stochastic Latent-State Estimation in Computational Psychiatry
items.abstract: Longitudinal computational psychiatry aims to build computer models that track how a person's hidden mental health state changes over time using incomplete real-world clues like daily symptoms, behavior, physical data, and environment. While standard time-series models are great for tracking changing systems, they often break down when the number of hidden variables is large, measurements are missing, and different types of uncertainty overlap. This paper introduces a new method to estimate these hidden states cleanly and efficiently by breaking down complex updates into a sequence of simple, structured approximations.What Problem This SolvesTracking hidden mental states: In psychiatry, clinicians cannot directly measure a patient's underlying neurobiological or psychological state. Instead, models must infer these hidden states from indirect signals like smartphone usage, heart rate, sleep patterns, and self-reported mood.Handling messy, high-dimensional data: Real-world patient data is often incomplete, noisy, and spans many interacting variables. Updating a model's estimate of a patient's state when new data arrives requires complex calculations that become slow and unreliable as the number of variables grows.Borrowing from data compression: The authors adapt a technique originally designed for compressing images in generative AI. Instead of compressing pixels, they use the same logic to compress and simplify the adjustments a model makes when updating its belief about a patient's mental state.How the Sequential Codebook Method WorksDefining the update target: Whenever new patient data arrives, the model needs to adjust its previous estimate of the patient's hidden state. This adjustment is called the posterior state correction, and the goal is to approximate it using a limited, efficient amount of information.Building a menu of candidate updates: Rather than searching through infinite possibilities to fix its estimate, the model generates several independent "sections," or groups, of random candidate adjustments. Each candidate is shaped to respect the natural correlations and uncertainty patterns among the patient's hidden variables.Picking the best match step by step: In the first section, the model compares all available candidates against the current estimation error (the residual) and picks the single candidate that aligns best with what needs to be fixed. It then subtracts that adjustment and moves to the next section to fix whatever error remains.Predictable error reduction: Under ideal conditions, the authors prove that each sequential step reduces the remaining estimation error by a reliable, predictable fraction. Because each section works independently on the leftover error, adding more sections steadily shrinks the overall mistake at a guaranteed rate.Accounting for real-world digital limits: In theory, the weight given to each chosen candidate could be any continuous number. In practice, computers must round these weights to finite digital values (quantization), so the authors explicitly calculate how this rounding affects accuracy.Real-World Extensions and SafeguardsHandling missing data and shifting conditions: Longitudinal studies frequently suffer from missed check-ins or dead wearable batteries. The framework is expanded to handle missing data types and to remain accurate even when a patient's data patterns shift away from what the model originally expected.Clear rules and failure modes: The authors lay out the exact conditions required for their error-reduction guarantees to hold. They also examine when the model might fail or struggle to tell two different hidden causes apart (identifiability).A roadmap for testing: The authors emphasize that this framework is a proposed research method, not a ready-to-use clinical tool. To prove its worth, it must be tested on unseen patient data, checked for reliable uncertainty estimates, stripped down to test which parts actually matter, and compared directly against traditional tracking models.Core TakeawayBridging statistics and state estimation: The paper's main theoretical breakthrough is linking the statistics of extreme values in random bell-curve samples (Gaussian order statistics) to step-by-step error reduction. This provides a mathematically grounded way to update complex, uncertainty-weighted models of human mental health.

items.title: Sharing Authority - How the GND network strives to integrate further communities to enrich its authority files.
items.abstract: Authority Files in the Age of AI: Building Trustworthy Information Through Collaboration As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes how we conduct research and retrieve information, the need for trustworthy and reliable information has never been greater. Authority files have long played a vital role in improving precision and recall in information retrieval, traditionally in bibliographic catalogues and increasingly in research data as well. But what potential do they hold for AI applications, and how can they help ensure that AI systems provide reliable information? This presentation explores the role of authority files as a foundation for trustworthy AI applications. It highlights the importance of bringing together the knowledge and expertise of diverse communities to create a broader and more inclusive network of reference entities – without compromising the reliability and quality of the data. Using the cooperative framework of the Gemeinsame Normdatei (GND) as an example, the presentation introduces an integrative infrastructure that enables communities to contribute their expertise to the collaborative creation and maintenance of authority data. Discover how collaboration, shared expertise and reliable authority data can help shape a more trustworthy information landscape in the age of AI. items.title: SheetAlign: Grounded Interaction and Stage-Isolated Learning for Spreadsheet Agents
items.abstract: Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making. Automating spreadsheet analysis while protecting sensitive data and controlling deployment costs motivates locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, complex spreadsheet tasks require both task reasoning and workbook understanding, while predefined operation interfaces impose additional tool-selection and invocation demands. We introduce SheetAlign, a spreadsheet manipulation framework with stage-isolated policy learning, organized around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement transformations. Task-guided inspection and API grounding anchor code generation in workbook observations and available operations, while stage-isolated learning optimizes program generation and review using edit-progress rewards. At inference, execution consistency selects programs through agreement among workbook states. On SpreadsheetBench, our grounded task interface improves Qwen3-4B's accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% on average without training. With learning and execution consistency, SheetAlign achieves 32.8% accuracy on average on SpreadsheetBench and 30.1% on Domain-Spreadsheet, outperforming comparable baselines. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.

items.title: SiliconGym: A Versatile Reinforcement Learning Environment for Agentic EDA
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with electronic design automation (EDA) feedback is advancing large language models for hardware design and verification. Extending these gains to hardware-engineering agents requires environments that span tasks, preserve state across tool calls, and support large hierarchies alongside parallel rollouts. We present SiliconGym, the first versatile, cross-task and cross-toolchain RL environment for hardware design and verification. By decoupling versioned workspaces, budgeted execution, and acceptance-gated scoring, SiliconGym scales from module-level RTL, testbench, and PPA tasks to multi-round repository repair and full-hierarchy SoC flows. Streaming dispatch overlaps tool checks with generation, finishing a 256-answer RL batch 21.9% faster than native ChipSeek. Using interchangeable open-source and commercial backends, we show that open-source-trained functional correctness transfers cleanly to commercial simulation, while paired netlist evaluation reveals when open-source PPA gains survive commercial synthesis.

items.title: Sirius-Tiamat: How Small Can a One-Pass Decision Encoder Get Before Its Decisions Change?
items.abstract: A one-pass decision encoder reads a text, a question and several named options, and returns a probability for each option in a single forward pass. We ask how far Laya, a 421M-parameter encoder of this kind, can be compressed before its decisions change. We count decisions that differ from Laya's own full-precision (fp32) answer, and track calibration (how well confidence matches accuracy, measured by expected calibration error, ECE), on 1,221 synthetic items with the training schemas, 273 with an unseen schema, and 800 out-of-family questions from ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag. Layer pruning of a related model family is known; we add flips, calibration, held-out data and retraining. bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family decisions but 2.2% out of family; 6-bit grouped rounding 1.3% and 5.9%; deleting 6 layers 0.9% and 9.1%, while ECE rises from 5.9% to 39.2%. One fitted temperature, needing no labels, restores it to 3.6%. One scale per tensor fails below six bits, and CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, nearly all through one layer. Total variation tracks flips for rounding but not for deletion, and an early exit saves layers over a static cut only if its confidence gate is first recalibrated. Distilling a 16-layer student cuts its in-family flips from 44% to 9% (45% out of family). At equal stored size, rounding flips fewer decisions than deletion. items.title: Sittisart (Rights-Centric Framework): A Foundational Governance Standard for Human Sovereignty in Artificial Intelligence Systems
items.abstract: Modern artificial intelligence paradigm designs overwhelmingly prioritize performance metrics, optimization velocity, and computational efficiency, reducing human oversight to post-hoc compliance mechanisms. This paper presents Sittisart (Rights-Centric Framework), a governance standard engineered to re-establish human sovereignty as the primary, non-negotiable axiom of artificial intelligence architecture. Sittisart posits that human autonomy over personal data, context interpretation, and final decision-making must structurally precede algorithmic performance. We articulate a Four-Layer Rights Architecture (R1–R4)—comprising Data Sovereignty, Consent Integrity, Interpretation Rights, and the Right to Cut—complemented by Three System Integrity Laws. Together, these frameworks define verifiable operational boundaries that prevent opaque inference, silent profiling, and semantic collapse in intelligent systems, establishing a standardized blueprint for privacy-preserving, human-aligned AI deployment.

items.title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
items.abstract: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png

items.title: Smartglasses Versus Smartphones for Video-Assisted Dispatcher-Guided CPR in Simulated Paediatric Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Video-assisted CPR (V-CPR) improves the quality of CPR. Nevertheless, the available evidence has focused primarily on adult cardiac arrest scenarios and on compression-dominated resuscitation manoeuvres. In the paediatric setting, where ventilation is critical, the usefulness of V-CPR has scarcely been explored. We aimed to compare V-CPR using smartglasses and/or smartphones with each other and with voice-only assistance via smartphone in a simulated paediatric cardiac arrest. Methods: In this experimental pilot simulation study, thirty-four undergraduate sports science students without BLS training in the previous two years participated in a simulated cardiac arrest of an 8-year-old child, under dispatcher guidance. Participants received video-assistance using smartglasses (VA-SG), video-assistance using a smartphone (VA-Ph), or voice-only assistance (C). They performed 5 min of CPR (30:2 ratio). Assessments included CPR quality, response times, and CPR skills. Results: We showed that VA-Ph and VA-SG outperformed C in most outcomes. Significant differences were observed in the number of effective ventilations (p = 0.010) and chest compressions (CC) at correct depth (p = 0.006). Ventilation quality was 37.1 ± 32.9% in C, 70.1 ± 30.7% in VA-Ph, and 66.3 ± 28.9% in VA-SG (p = 0.038). CC quality reached 55.6 ± 28.0% in C, 74.0 ± 22.9% in VA-Ph, and 77.9 ± 16.6% in VA-SG (p = 0.150). Overall CPR quality was numerically higher in both video-assisted groups, although the difference was not statistically significant. V-CPR also improved correct CC hand placement (p = 0.001) and airway opening (p = 0.036). Response times did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusions: Video-assistance via smartglasses or smartphones improves key components of the quality of dispatcher-guided CPR during simulated paediatric cardiac arrest, doubling effective ventilations and improving the proportion of compressions at correct depth, with no significant differences in time to CPR initiation. Direct scene visualisation gives dispatchers better situational awareness, enabling more accurate, real-time guidance that could translate into higher-quality resuscitation and improved outcomes.

items.title: Socioeconomic Status and AI Use for Schoolwork in Relation to Adolescents’ School Belonging and Loneliness in Four Chinese Regions
items.abstract: Socioeconomic differences in adolescents’ school belonging and school loneliness are important concerns for psychological adjustment. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into schoolwork, its associations with students’ school experiences and the moderating roles of relational resources warrant examination. This study used cross-sectional PISA data from adolescents in four Chinese regions. Unweighted multiple linear regression analyses examined economic, social and cultural status (ESCS) and AI use for schoolwork in relation to school loneliness and school belonging. Family support and peer academic help-seeking were examined separately as moderators of the associations between ESCS and each outcome. All models included sex, age, and school fixed effects. Multiple testing was addressed using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Higher ESCS and more frequent AI use for schoolwork were associated with lower school loneliness and greater school belonging. Peer academic help-seeking moderated the association between ESCS and school loneliness after FDR correction. The negative association weakened as peer academic help-seeking increased. Family support did not significantly moderate either association, and peer academic help-seeking did not significantly moderate the association between ESCS and school belonging. These findings suggest a limited compensatory role for peer academic help-seeking in socioeconomic differences in school loneliness, providing partial support for the resource compensation perspective.

items.title: Soil salinity: Recent advances and future prospects
items.abstract: Soil salinity is one of the major environmental constraints limiting agricultural productivity and global food security, affecting approximately 833 M ha of land worldwide. Its extent is increasing due to climate change, seawater intrusion, rock weathering, poor irrigation practices, inadequate drainage, groundwater over-extraction, excessive fertiliser use, irrigation with saline water and industrial effluent discharge. Salinity degrades soil structure, reduces nutrient availability, impairs photosynthesis, restricts plant growth and ultimately decreases crop productivity. This review provides a comprehensive and up-to-date synthesis of the causes, impacts, assessment methods and management strategies for soil salinity while highlighting recent advances in biotechnology and precision agriculture. Unlike previous reviews that focus on individual aspects of salinity, this review integrates conventional and emerging approaches within a single framework. Relevant literature was systematically identified and screened using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology to ensure transparent and comprehensive coverage. Recent advances in salinity assessment include remote sensing, electromagnetic induction (EMI), machine learning and geospatial techniques, enabling accurate large-scale monitoring and management of salt-affected soils. Effective mitigation strategies include improved irrigation and drainage, mulching, chemical amendments, silicon (Si) application, beneficial microorganisms, phytoremediation, nanotechnology and integrated soil management. Biotechnological approaches such as marker-assisted breeding, molecular breeding and CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing have accelerated the development of salt-tolerant crop varieties, including BRRI dhan73, BRRI dhan99, CSR 101 and CSR 104. Future research should prioritise climate-resilient agriculture, sustainable land reclamation, precision farming and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven technologies to enhance long-term salinity management and food security.
