items.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
items.abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

items.title: Spatiotemporal shoreline and sea level dynamics along the Kenyan coast (2000–2024): patterns of erosion, accretion, and spatial autocorrelation
items.abstract: Shoreline management in the Western Indian Ocean (WIO) is largely informed by small-scale studies with coarse temporal resolution, potentially obscuring fine spatial patterns and interannual dynamics. This study examines spatiotemporal shoreline change along 400 km of the Kenyan coastline from 2000 to 2024 and tests its association with regional sea-level trend and variability, accounting for spatial dependence. Twenty-five annual Landsat-derived shoreline positions were analyzed using the Digital Shoreline Analysis System (DSAS) along 12,455 transects using Weighted Linear Regression (WLR) weighted by a tide- and registration-based positional uncertainty of approximately 40 to 68 m per epoch. Sea-level predictors were derived from GLORYS12V1 reanalysis at its native grid (47 coastal cells) and tested with Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), a Spatial Lag Model (SLM), and Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR). Results reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity. The Kilifi and Kwale–Mombasa zones show net accretion (mean WLR 0.57 and 0.51 m yr -1 , respectively), whereas the Tana–Manda zone shows net erosion (mean WLR = −0.92 m yr −1 ), with 36.23% of its transects significantly eroding. The national mean Net Shoreline Movement of +9.45 m obscures this variability. Shoreline change is strongly spatially autocorrelated (Moran’s I = 0.866, p = 0.001) and 12.01% of transects form statistically significant local clusters (6.23% as High–High accretion and 5.57% Low–Low erosion clusters). Neither sea-level trend nor sea-level variability showed a detectable association with shoreline change at the native support of the predictors (OLS R 2 ≤ 0.028, p ≥ 0.26; SLM not significant; GWR adjusted R 2 < 0). At the scales resolved here, shoreline change along the Kenyan coast is therefore not explained by regional sea-level variation and is more plausibly linked to local geomorphic and human factors. National averages must be complemented by spatially explicit, uncertainty-weighted assessments to inform shoreline management policy.

items.title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember
items.abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

items.title: Static Analysis Guidance for Secure LLM Code Generation
items.abstract: Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.

items.title: Study on Quantitative Modeling of Task Completion Probability in AI Agents Using DAG and State-Machine
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly decompose user instructions into task lists, but widely used approaches (AutoGPT, BabyAGI, MetaGPT) generate simple linear, ID-ordered sequences that cannot express conditional branching or parallel execution. Newer orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, the LLM Compiler, and the Claude Agent SDK add DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) or state-machine execution control for non-linear workflows, yet none provides a quantitative, probabilistic estimate of how likely a plan is to succeed, or how much a redundant (alternative) path improves that likelihood. This study integrates DAG-based dependency modeling, prompt engineering for conditional branching, and a state-machine execution engine, and formulates the resulting task-completion probability P(Goal) with reliability engineering. The model is generalized to 1-out-of-n (parallel) path redundancy and to general DAG topologies with parallel branching and AND-joins, and a cost-constrained redundancy-allocation problem and a Beta-prior estimator of path success probabilities from execution logs are given. Assuming independent task outcomes, Monte Carlo simulations (10,000–100,000 trials) of a retrieval-and-summarization task (72.7% completion for the linear model, 84.4% with redundancy) agree with the closed-form predictions to within 0.18 percentage points across 24 parameter combinations and within 1 point under all conditions. Redundancy at the bottleneck stage yields about 3.9 times the gain at the most reliable stage, as the marginal-utility formula predicts. Alternative paths help most when failures are persistent; correlated failures reduce the gain. With a real LLM agent (100 runs), completion rates predicted from probabilities estimated on half the runs fell within the 95% intervals observed on the other half.

items.title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
items.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the scope of the AI Act.

items.title: Success Stories of Tech-Savvy Teachers in Crafting Lesson Plans with Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Teachers increasingly use generative artificial intelligence to prepare lessons, yet few accounts describe how teachers who are comfortable with digital tools do this successfully, what they still need, and how this looks in Philippine schools. This study documented the experiences of tech-savvy teachers in crafting lesson plans with artificial intelligence, the digital competencies they credited for their success, the challenges and strategies they reported, and the institutional support they recommended. A qualitative exploratory-descriptive design was used. Fifteen teachers of languages, mathematics, social science and social studies, organization and management, and agriculture, with 1 year 8 months to 16 years of teaching experience, were recruited through convenience and referral sampling and answered an online open-ended questionnaire. Tool use was summarized with frequencies and percentages, and the 58 written responses were analyzed through thematic analysis. ChatGPT (80%) and Google Gemini (66.7%) were the most used tools. Four themes emerged. First, fourteen teachers described planning with artificial intelligence as faster, easier, and more productive, and two noted effort at the outset, mainly in writing prompts. Second, success was linked to foundational digital literacy, prompt writing, and the ability to evaluate output, used together with teaching judgment. Third, the main challenges were output that did not fit learners, inaccurate information, and over-reliance, which teachers managed by reviewing, verifying, and localizing output. Fourth, teachers asked for continuous training, peer collaboration, and clear guidelines on appropriate use and its declaration. Interpreted through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework and technology acceptance theory, the findings suggest that these teachers’ success rested on their own judgment, prompting skill, and the support available to them. Because of the small sample, the brevity of many responses, and signs that some responses were machine-assisted, the findings are exploratory and not generalizable.

items.title: Sustainable Entrepreneurial Education and Entrepreneurial Intention in the Generative AI Era
items.abstract: Sustainability-oriented entrepreneurship education is gaining traction, but few studies examine the mechanisms by which learning experiences translate into intentions to create socially and environmentally responsible businesses. Based on Human Capital Theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour, this research investigates the mediating effect of sustainable opportunity recognition and green creativity sequentially and the moderating effect of Generative AI Literacy for Learning. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyse the survey responses of 407 students from public and private universities in Punjab, Pakistan. The findings showed a positive correlation between educational exposure and opportunity identification, which is linked to creative idea generation and, in turn, higher entrepreneurial intentions. The indirect (sequential) relationship is significant. Moreover, GenAI literacy strengthens both the education–intention and creativity–intention relationships, suggesting that technological competence complements sustainability-focused learning. These findings complement the existing explanations of entrepreneurial intention by adding an extension of the cognitive and creative process to a technology-related boundary condition. The study also underscores the importance of integrating sustainability problems, opportunities, innovative problem-solving, and responsible leveraging of generative AI into the curriculum, especially for higher education institutions, which are crucial for nurturing entrepreneurial aspirations in today's learning landscape.

items.title: Systematic Literature Review: Digital Transformation with AI Integration in Vocational Education and Practices (2021-2025)
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the challenges, implementation strategies, and benefits of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into vocational education and practice from 2021 to 2025. A systematic literature review was conducted using the PRISMA approach. Data were collected from the Scopus database. A Total of 17 articles met the inclusion criteria and then were analyzed using the PICOC framework. Findings indicate that the adoption of AI in vocational education and training not only faces technical issues but also challenges related to human readiness, institutional capacity, digital literacy, infrastructure gaps, and unequal access between developed and developing countries. Effective AI implementation requires an integrated strategy involving adaptive curriculum design, continuous training for educators, institutional leadership, industry collaboration, and the development of a supportive digital ecosystem. The integration of AI offers significant benefits in enhancing the quality of learning, the effectiveness of training, competency alignment, and workplace readiness, but its impact depends on how well the technology aligns with pedagogy, institutional readiness, and industry needs. Overall, the success of AI integration cannot be measured only by the technology used, but also by the capabilities of educational institutions and the creation of a collaborative ecosystem that is valuable to industry.

items.title: Teaching Reform of Civil Engineering Construction Course under the Background of AI
items.abstract: With the large-scale implementation of generative artificial intelligence, digital twin, BIM and other technologies in the construction industry, the construction industry is transforming from the traditional manual construction mode to the intelligent construction mode, and the demand for industry post ability has changed significantly. As a core compulsory course of civil engineering undergraduate major, civil engineering construction undertakes the task of imparting professional knowledge such as construction technology, construction organization and site management. The traditional classroom teaching mode has practical contradictions such as lack of practical scenes, lagging update of teaching content, insufficient individualized training of students, and single assessment method. The teaching practice shows that the reasonable introduction of AI auxiliary tools can make up for the shortcomings of traditional teaching field conditions, enrich classroom case resources, and strengthen students’ engineering practice thinking. However, it also faces practical challenges such as students’ excessive dependence on AI output content, professional information distortion, and teachers’ teaching ability can not keep up with technical iteration. This study can provide reference for the digital teaching reform of construction courses in similar engineering majors, and help to cultivate compound civil engineering talents with both traditional construction skills and intelligent construction literacy.

items.title: Technological and Organisational Readiness for Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Organisational Innovation in Deposit Money Banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Banks in emerging economies are under pressure to deliver faster, more personalised and more efficient digital financial services, yet many struggle to convert investments in artificial intelligence (AI) into innovation. This study examined how two dimensions of AI adoption readiness, technological readiness and organisational readiness, relate to product innovation and process innovation in deposit money banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and the Resource-Based View, the study adopted a descriptive, cross-sectional, correlational survey of 400 employees and managers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. Respondents rated organisational readiness (M = 3.62), process innovation (M = 3.59), product innovation (M = 3.54) and technological readiness (M = 3.45) above the scale midpoint. Both readiness dimensions correlated strongly and positively with both innovation outcomes (r = .68 to .74, p < .001). In multiple regression, the two predictors jointly explained 57.5% of the variance in product innovation and 56.7% in process innovation, and organisational readiness had the larger standardised coefficient in both models (β = .535 and .444) compared with technological readiness (β = .263 and .353). The findings indicate that technology is necessary but not sufficient for AI-enabled innovation. Banks should pair investment in infrastructure and skills with leadership sponsorship, employee training, a supportive culture and strategic alignment.

items.title: Tecnologías digitales en la educación universitaria: revisión sistemática sobre oportunidades, desafíos y tendencias educativas
items.abstract: Context: The acceleration of digital transformation has reshaped learning environments in higher education and the conditions under which teachers and students engage in the learning process. This transformation creates opportunities while also posing challenges related to digital competencies, equity, and technological governance. Objective: To analyze the opportunities, challenges, and educational trends associated with the use of digital technologies in higher education. Method: A systematic literature review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and the Population, Interest, and Context (PICo) framework. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, SciELO, ERIC, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 25 empirical studies published between 2022 and September 2026. Results: The findings identified learning flexibility and personalization, the early adoption of generative artificial intelligence, and the growing importance of teachers' digital competence as major educational trends. Disparities in access were also observed, influenced by technological infrastructure and training opportunities. Blended learning and ethical technology governance emerged as key elements in guiding institutional transformation. Conclusions: The effective pedagogical integration of digital technologies in higher education requires coherent institutional policies, continuous professional development for faculty members, and critical digital literacy across the university community. Technological transformation must be accompanied by strategies aimed at narrowing digital access gaps and ensuring educational integration that is contextually relevant, equitable, and responsible.

items.title: TECNOLOGIAS EMERGENTES E PRÁTICAS BASEADAS EM EVIDÊNCIAS NA FISIOTERAPIA DO TRABALHO E ERGONOMIA: DA PREVENÇÃO DE RISCOS OCUPACIONAIS À ALTA PERFORMANCE
items.abstract: As transformações tecnológicas associadas à Indústria 4.0, à saúde digital e à inteligência artificial ampliaram o repertório da Fisioterapia do Trabalho e da Ergonomia, permitindo que avaliações antes pontuais sejam complementadas por monitoramento contínuo, análise automatizada de posturas e intervenções remotas. Este trabalho discute, sob a perspectiva da prática baseada em evidências, o papel de sensores vestíveis, unidades de medição inercial, inteligência artificial, visão computacional, exoesqueletos ocupacionais, telereabilitação, estações de trabalho ativas e programas de exercício no enfrentamento dos distúrbios osteomusculares relacionados ao trabalho. A revisão priorizou estudos indexados publicados entre 2020 e 2026, com ênfase em revisões sistemáticas, meta-análises, ensaios clínicos e revisões de escopo, além da Norma Regulamentadora nº 17 como referência normativa brasileira. Os achados mostram que intervenções ergonômicas e exercício no local de trabalho possuem evidência mais consolidada para redução de dor e melhora funcional; tecnologias vestíveis e sistemas automatizados ampliam a capacidade de mensurar exposição biomecânica em tempo real, mas ainda apresentam heterogeneidade de validação; exoesqueletos reduzem carga muscular em tarefas específicas, embora conforto, adaptação e transferência dos resultados de laboratório para o campo permaneçam limitadas; e a telereabilitação apresenta resultados clínicos comparáveis ou favoráveis em diferentes condições musculoesqueléticas. Conclui-se que a alta performance ocupacional deve ser entendida como desempenho sustentável, com preservação da saúde, redução de fadiga, retorno seguro ao trabalho e melhor capacidade funcional, e não como intensificação indiscriminada da produção. A integração tecnológica é mais efetiva quando subordinada à análise ergonômica, à participação do trabalhador e à tomada de decisão clínica baseada na melhor evidência disponível.

items.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

items.title: The AI Explainability Paradox in Cybersecurity: Does More Explanation Improve or Impair Human Decisions?
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important area of research as AI systems are increasingly used to support cybersecurity decisions. Providing explanations for AI-generated recommendations can improve transparency, help users understand system outputs, and support greater confidence in automated decisions. However, increasing the amount of information provided by an AI system may also create additional cognitive demands for users, particularly when explanations contain complex technical information. This paper examines the AI explainability paradox in cybersecurity, focusing on the relationship between explanation complexity, cognitive load, human understanding, and security decision-making. Drawing on existing literature related to explainable AI, cognitive load, human-AI interaction, cybersecurity decision-making, and technology trust, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI explanation, information complexity, cognitive load, user understanding, verification behaviour, and decision quality. The paper proposes that effective explainability should not be determined only by the amount of information provided, but also by the ability of users to understand and effectively use that information during security-related decisions. While appropriate explanations may improve transparency and support informed judgement, excessive or technically complex explanations may increase cognitive load and reduce decision effectiveness. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI explanation influence human cybersecurity decisions and contributes to the development of human-centred explainable AI systems.

items.title: The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets
items.abstract: Today, businesses are making more and more use of Artificial Intelligent (AI) technologies in their operations. This widespread use of AI technologies is changing how a consumer searches, evaluates and purchases products in the online intelligent markets. Consumer behavior is shaped by consumer’s own cognition as well as influence by machine learning systems (AI technologies). These advanced systems use algorithmic personalization, predictive analysis, ranking systems and automated decision support to guide the consumers. To understand the consumer buying behavior in these intelligent markets, this paper, titled “The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets,” proposes an integrated conceptual framework. “Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) (Venkatesh et al. 2003)”, “Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers, 2003)” and “Disruptive Innovation Perspectives (Christensen, 1997)” are the foundations of this research. This paper argues that the algorithmic influence works through three interconnected mechanisms namely, behavioral reinforcement through personalization, cognitive effort reduction and perceived performance enhancement. Here, conventional consumer behavior models are extended by adding new constructs such as algorithmic trust, perceived AI transparency, adaptive habit formation and data-driven social influence. This paper proposes that AI tools and systems do not simply play the role of marketing tools but also actively influence consumer preferences, attention, post-purchase learning and habits. In this work, theory is being built methodologically and conceptual synthesis technique is used. Model abstraction (simplification) and comparison analysis is used to achieve proposed conceptual integration. A through multidisciplinary analysis which included literature from marketing, information systems and innovation studies, was carried out. The aim of this exercise was to identify overlapping theoretical frameworks. With this exercise a nested framework is created that connect behavioral results, psychological mediators and technology affordances. Traditional consumer theories have been used, which focus on the human-centric framework as a base for this exercise. This base was further expanded to understand AI-augmented viewpoint. This study strongly proposes that AI tools & systems are actively involved in the consumer’s decisions-making journey as opposed to the previous conception of them being simply passive actors, guiding consumers. The implications of this study highlight that organizations must manage system transparency, trust alignment and personalization to maximize consumer engagement. This study describes “algorithmic consumer” and its inception. Going further, this study also lays foundation for future empirical studies as well as policy discussions of autonomy, ethics, and control over pricing in the AI-powered digital ecosystems.

items.title: The application of deep learning-based artificial intelligence for accurate lymphatic vessel identification in indocyanine green imaging
items.abstract: Objective: This study aims to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) system based on the U-Net deep learning architecture to automatically identify and stage lymphatic vessels in indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography images, thereby enhancing recognition efficiency and objectivity and assisting in the planning of lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) surgery. Methods: A total of 560 ICG lymphography images from 140 patients with lower-limb lymphedema were collected. After standard preprocessing, the images were randomly split into a training set and a test set in a 7:3 ratio. The U-Net model was used for training, with hyperparameters optimized using a five-fold cross-validation approach. The Adam optimizer was employed for model training. Evaluation metrics included precision, recall, F1 score, and inference time. Results: The model demonstrated excellent performance in identifying lymphatic vessels across lymphedema stages I–IV. The precision scores for each stage were as follows: stage I: 95.29%, stage II: 92.58%, stage III: 93.17%, and stage IV: 90.08%. Recall rates for all stages were above 89%, and all F1 scores exceeded 90%, indicating strong overall accuracy and balance between precision and recall. The average inference time per image was just 56 milliseconds, highlighting the model’s suitability for near-real-time applications. Additionally, the confusion matrix revealed a high discriminative capability across the different lymphedema stages. Conclusion: The U-Net-based AI model demonstrated high accuracy and efficiency in the automatic identification of lymphatic vessels in ICG images, highlighting its strong potential for clinical applications. This system may significantly support LVA surgical planning, enable real-time intraoperative navigation, and serve as a valuable tool for physician training.

items.title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

items.title: The Digitalisation of Construction (2016–2025): A Critical Narrative Review of BIM, AI, Robotics and Digital Twins: Evidence Maturity, Circular Economy Disconnect and a Research Agenda
items.abstract: Research on construction digitalisation has grown quickly but remains fragmented. This narrative review examines Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 2016 and 2025 on Building Information Modelling (BIM), artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, digital twins and related automation. A pool of 494 records was screened by title, abstract and keywords, and 89 articles were retained. An eligibility audit then separated 78 core studies from 11 records in which digital technology was contextual. The review combines a descriptive profile of the literature with an explicit, criteria based assessment of evidence maturity and of circular economy linkage. This narrative review used a single database and screening by one reviewer. Exclusion followed a construct based relevance test and not study quality. The exact date of the Scopus search was not recorded. Output accelerated after 2022 (74.2% of the 89 articles appeared from 2023 to 2025), 77.5% appeared in two MDPI journals, and author affiliations were concentrated in China and the United Kingdom. Nine overlapping themes emerged, led by BIM for design, coordination and compliance (39 core studies), robotics, automation and additive manufacturing (30), and AI and machine learning (24). Six records addressed circularity or waste reduction, and only two applied a digital tool to a material recovery or waste outcome. Within the retrieved sample, the link to the circular economy is therefore a thin evidence base and not an established finding, and the low count may partly reflect the search strategy. Case studies, pilots and cross sectional surveys are common (19 and 16 of the 89 screened records, respectively), whereas longitudinal studies and multisite validation appear limited. Blockchain evidence in the sample is minimal. A research agenda is proposed for validated, integrated and context-sensitive studies.

items.title: The Dilemma of Authorship in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Drawing the Line Between AI-Generated and AI-Assisted Works in Copyright Law from a Sri Lankan Perspective
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has destabilised an assumption embedded in copyright doctrine: that the person who communicates instructions to a machine is also the person who creates the resulting expression. This article examines where Sri Lankan copyright law should draw the line between AI-generated and AI-assisted literary and artistic works. Employing doctrinal and comparative methods, it analyses the Intellectual Property Act, No. 36 of 2003, leading Sri Lankan originality decisions and approaches adopted in the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union and India. It argues that the statutory requirement of a physical-person author prevents attribution of authorship to an autonomous system, but does not preclude protection for sufficiently original human contributions embodied in an AI-mediated work. It proposes a five-stage Human Creative Contribution Test, proceeding through attribution, expressive specification, effective control and causation, originality, and protection and allocation. The proposed model avoids both automatic copyright for every prompt and indiscriminate denial of protection whenever AI has assisted a human creator. It further recommends evidential disclosure, clarification of partial protection and carefully framed statutory guidance rather than the immediate introduction of machine authorship.

items.title: The effect of response typing speed on trust in AI chat interfaces
items.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence systems has become increasingly important as these systems assume advisory and decision-support roles. The present studies examine whether the temporal presentation of artificial intelligence (AI) generated responses, specifically typing animation speed, affects trust in chat-based interfaces. In Experiment 1, participants ( N = 71) interacted with three AI agents using pre-scripted question-response pairs detailing different facts about exotic animals. Response presentation speed (slow, fast, or instant) was manipulated within subjects. Results showed that compared to instant presentation, typing animations significantly increased trust in the AI agent but not trust in individual responses. Experiment 2 ( N = 68) employed similar procedures but used a live language model and allowed participants to generate their own questions. Under these more naturalistic conditions, presentation speed influenced both measures of trust, with typing animations consistently producing higher trust than instant presentation. These findings demonstrate that temporal presentation features can systematically shape trust judgments independent of content quality.

items.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship
items.abstract: Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

items.title: THE EVOLUTION AND IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
items.abstract: This concept paper explores the evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within foreign language education, specifically examining the transition from Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) to Intelligent Computer-Assisted Language Learning (ICALL). Current research indicates that AI technologies, such as Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP), are being utilized to provide personalized learning experiences, automated feedback, and sophisticated assessment tools. While these tools demonstrate significant pedagogical benefits, including improved language proficiency and increased learner autonomy, challenges remain regarding teacher preparation, technological reliability, and ethical implications. This paper proposes a framework to effectively integrate AI into pedagogy, repositioning the teacher as a facilitator and mentor in an AI-enhanced environment.

items.title: The Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology: A Methodological Shift from the Perspective of Natural Science and Engineering Practice
items.abstract: Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, fundamentally driven by the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm, rely on setting external objectives and iterative trial-and-error. When confronted with complex nonlinear problems containing noise and conflicting constraints, this paradigm inherently induces statistical smoothing and compromise, yielding black-box models that lack interpretability and out-of-distribution generalization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology, reconstructing the solving process into four irreversible stages: Deconstruction, Structure, Construction, and Solving. The method suspends a priori presuppositions to strip unit coupling, extracts rigid invariants inherent to the problem, constructs equivalent mappings anchored to these invariants, and executes the mapping directly to generate the solution. Evaluation metrics and experience are relegated to a posteriori verification. Demonstrated through cross-disciplinary practices including number theory, Hamiltonian systems, deep learning, and seismic inversion, this methodology transcends the statistical fitting bottleneck. Structure-Driven and Objective-Driven methodologies are complementary: when structure is sufficient, solutions are directly constructed; when lacking, it degenerates into the OD path.

items.title: The Governance Frontier COBIT-Aligned AI Decision Support and Risk-Adaptive Optimization for Enterprise Technology Modernization
items.abstract: Executives deciding enterprise modernization, legacy-system transformation, AI adoption, organizational restructuring, digital-infrastructure change, and cross-functional governance must weigh legal, financial, cybersecurity, procurement, opera-tional, and AI-governance questions that sit in separate functions. The central methods of this paper are GAIM-DF (Governance-Aware Institutional Modernization Decision Framework), a human-gated advisory process for these decisions, and Risk-Adaptive AI Governance Optimization (RA-GO v2), a risk-adaptive optimizer with mandatory governance gates, halt-safe feasibility, distributionally robust evaluation, and preference-information triage for scarce human review; an accountable human decides. As an optional architectural extension, we compu-tationally evaluate a multi-expert coordination layer that convenes specialist capabilities by context and consolidates constraints conservatively. Evidence is staged across four complementary pre-deployment approaches: analytical verification; retrospective historical-data analysis; comparative computational benchmark-ing against strong baselines; and scenario-based stress testing under distributional shift. Together they provide complementary pre-deployment evidence for high-stakes governance analysis. A systematic review of university and public-sector governance, with observational process-log analyses and RA-GO scenario stress tests, yields six principal findings: role coordination is associated with shorter approval and process times under supporting falsification checks; robust evaluation preserves tail-risk protection under distribution shift; preference-information triage concentrates human review where it most reduces modeled regret; and mandatory gates, an intensity floor, and a halt state are jointly consistent. The multi-expert benchmarks report accuracy, false-positive, latency, and token-cost trade-offs and routing failure modes relative to a strong Single-Agent baseline and to RA-GO alone. Shadow-mode piloting and a risk-adaptive Hybrid remain future work.

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Intelligent Workplaces: AI Monitoring, Psychological Safety and Employee Trust
items.abstract: Employers are adopting software that tracks activity, scores behaviour and flags deviations, and surveys suggest that half of U.S. workers already believe they are monitored. This study asks what such monitoring is associated with in the places where trust and psychological safety are formed. It assembles the published results of two Harris Poll surveys for the American Psychological Association (2,515 workers in 2023 and 2,027 in 2024), Gallup’s September 2026 study of trust in leaders’ use of employee data, and Gallup’s 2026 workforce surveys on AI, and analyses them with explicit effect-size formulas: risk ratios, Cohen’s h, random-effects pooling, population attributable fractions and implied-rate bounds. Across ten published contrasts, monitored workers fared worse on every outcome, with a pooled effect size of h = 0.36 (95% interval 0.22 to 0.49 after allowing for correlated outcomes) and substantial heterogeneity (I-squared 70 percent). They were nearly twice as likely to plan to leave within a year (39 versus 21 percent; risk ratio 1.86, 95% interval 1.56 to 2.21), which would correspond to about 30 percent of such intentions if the association were causal. Trust in leaders’ use of employee data is low (20 percent a great deal) and steeply related to concern (13 to 65 percent across trust levels); only 19 percent of employees have ever been told what is collected, and conversations raise both trust and concern. The evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported and partly drawn from press summaries, so the findings are associations. Purpose - This study examines how AI-enabled workplace monitoring relates to psychological safety, trust and strain, and what published evidence implies about the conditions under which monitoring is tolerated. Design/methodology/approach - The paper reanalyses published survey contrasts from the American Psychological Association and Gallup using effect-size formulas, random-effects pooling with a correlation adjustment, replication tests across survey waves, attributable-fraction calculations and implied-rate bounds, with sensitivity checks for assumed group sizes and design effects. Findings - Monitoring is associated with higher strain, lower perceived respect and trust, and exit intentions; effects are heterogeneous but consistently positive. Trust in data use is closely tied to engagement and concern, and transparency raises trust and concern together. Research limitations/implications - Group sizes and design effects are approximated, some sources are secondary, and the data are cross-sectional self-reports with no causal identification or direct measure of psychological safety in the monitoring contrasts. Practical implications - Employers should specify what is monitored and why, involve workers in setting limits, keep humans in decisions that affect people, and expect transparency to raise questions before it builds trust. Social implications - Monitoring that workers read as distrust may carry costs in strain and turnover that are not visible in productivity dashboards. Originality/value - The paper combines two decades of theory on trust and psychological safety with the most recent U.S. survey evidence on AI-era monitoring and quantifies the size, heterogeneity and sensitivity of the reported associations.

items.title: The Human–AI Resource Dynamics Framework: A Structured Narrative Review of Employee Empowerment and Resource Depletion in AI-Enabled Manufacturing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping manufacturing work, offering opportunities for employee empowerment while introducing psychological and organizational demands. Using selected PRISMA 2020 reporting items to describe search and study selection, this structured narrative review draws on a final corpus of 16 empirical studies to develop the Human–AI Resource Dynamics (HARD) framework, integrating Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model. A theory-informed narrative synthesis identifies two potentially coexisting pathways with uneven empirical support. The Bright Empowering Path links psychological availability, self-efficacy, positive appraisals, and task fit with proactive behavior and performance. The proposed Dark Depleting Path organizes distinct associations involving hindrance appraisal, AI anxiety, job insecurity, and surveillance-related autonomy loss, rather than one empirically validated depletion chain. Individual, organizational, and technological conditions shape these relationships. Evidence for empowerment is comparatively more consistent, whereas depletion findings remain heterogeneous and primarily observational. Methodological diversity, geographical concentration, and limited longitudinal evidence constrain causal and cross-contextual conclusions. HARD provides an AI-specific integrative framework for future empirical testing and human-centered AI implementation within Industry 5.0.
